The water molecule is bent because of the arrangement of its electrons around the central oxygen atom.

Oxygen has six valence electrons. Two of them bond with the two hydrogen atoms, which leaves four electrons that form two lone pairs. So the oxygen is surrounded by four regions of electron density: two bonding pairs and two lone pairs.

These four regions push away from each other as far as they can, which gives a roughly tetrahedral arrangement with bond angles near 109.5°. The two lone pairs take up more space than the bonding pairs, though, so they squeeze the two O–H bonds closer together. The actual H–O–H angle ends up around 104.5°, which is why the molecule is bent rather than straight.

I can't display a 3D model from here, so picture a tetrahedron with two corners holding hydrogens and two corners holding lone pairs, with the lone pairs pushing the hydrogens toward each other.
